World.title: Marcos’ Japan state visit: Focus on security, energy cooperation
World.content:
This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article.

The Philippine President is set to embark on a rare state visit to Japan. Tokyo typically hosts — at most — just one state visit in a year.

MANILA, Philippines — When Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. arrives in Japan for a rare state visit, he will have two priorities in mind: the two Asian nations’ security cooperation given “coercion and gray-zone tactics” in the sea, and Manila’s energy security dreams in the wake of a global energy crisis caused by war in the Middle East.

The Philippine President, ahead of a scheduled state visit to Japan from May 26 to May 29, noted the Japan Self-Defense Forces’ (JSDF) recent participation in Balikatan 2026, the yearly war games between the Philippines and its treaty ally, the United States.

Play Video

“That is important because that changes the playing field, as it were. It changes it significantly. And for Japan now, I suppose you could say it is imperative that those, that new posture of Japan, we have to define it now in terms — and this is what I would seek to clarify — is to define it in terms of how it’s going to work for Japan and the Philippines bilaterally, and together, but multilaterally, together with our other friends and allies in the region. And this extends now for all the way to the Indo-Pacific,” said Marcos in an interview with Japanese media on Monday, May 18.

Marcos and his wife, First Lady Louise Araneta-Marcos, are set to travel to Japan for a state visit upon the invitation of the Japanese government. State visits are the highest level of foreign visits in most countries, including Japan.

Rare state visit

Tokyo typically only hosts one state visit a year, which involves a call on Japan’s Emperor and Empress, a state banquet for the visiting heads of state, as well as a summit or meeting with the Japanese Prime Minister.

In 2025, Japan hosted Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Japan did not host a state visit since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 until 2024. Prior to a worldwide lockdown due to COVID-19, the last world leader to be feted a state visit to Japan was United States President Donald Trump in his first presidential term of office.

Japan is the Philippines’ first, and for some time, only strategic partner. Manila has since expanded its web of strategic partners to include Vietnam, Australia, South Korea, and India. The latter three partnerships were signed only under Marcos, whose administration has been seeking an expansion of the Philippines’ defense and security partnerships.

Defense ties between the Philippines and Japan have been robust for years, long before the signing and eventual ratification of the Reciprocal Access Agreement (RAA), which paved the way for the JSDF to engage in war games. Japan is the largest source of Official Development Assistance to the Philippines. Manila was also the first recipient of Japan’s Official Security Assistance, making it a key partner in the Philippines’ military modernization efforts.

In January 2026, the Philippines and Japan signed an Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement, or a framework to govern the provision of supplies between the JSDF and the Armed Forces of the Philippines.

Energy resilience

Marcos also said Japan has “taken a more active role when it comes to the subject of energy and the energy supply.”

“We are actually very grateful to Japan because Japan has been of great assistance to us in trying to find different solutions for the supply of the different kinds of fuel. And that has become a critical part of our policy,” said Marcos.

The Philippines is among those in the region most affected by disruptions to the supply of oil and other petroleum products caused by the US and Israel’s war on Iran and the subsequent closing of the Strait of Hormuz. Before the February 2026 war, Manila sourced almost all its oil from the Middle East — either crude oil from the Gulf or petroleum products processed in Asia, but also from Middle Eastern crude oil.

In April 2026, Japan announced that it would provide up to US$10 billion in assistance through the Partnership on Wide Energy and Resources Resilience (POWERR Asia).

“And we will again try to get more clarity on what the POWERR Asia system that has been proposed by Prime Minister Takaichi. What does it mean in terms of linkages between our different countries, between the Philippines and Japan, and between all of the countries in the region?” said Marcos, who as chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), led an early May 2026 meeting of leaders to find a way for the bloc to better shield itself from energy supply disruptions and price fluctuations.

Marcos has been to Japan at least twice before as Philippine President — in early 2023 for an official visit and then in mid-2025 to visit the Philippine pavilion at the World Expo 2025 in Osaka, Japan. – Rappler.com

World.title: Court dismisses terrorism financing case vs Cebu NGO
World.content:
This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article.

STOP ATTACKS. Human rights advocates, labor leaders, and development workers from ADI, CERNET, NUPL Cebu, and Bayan Central Visayas speak to the media during a press conference in Cebu City on May 17, 2024.

CERNET says it would pursue criminal, administrative, and civil actions against those who sought the 'malicious and wrongful prosecution' of its members

CEBU, Philippines – A regional court in Cebu City has dismissed the terrorism financing case against 27 former and active members of Cebu-based non-governmental organization Community Empowerment Resource Network (CERNET).

In May 2024, the Department of Justice (DOJ) filed the complaint against them, alleging that CERNET violated the Terrorism Financing Prevention and Suppression Act of 2012 by providing P135,000 to the Communist Party of the Philippines-New People’s Army (CPP-NPA) in September 2012.

The ruling from the 7th Judicial Regional Trial Court Branch 74 in Cebu and signed by Judge Van Russel Inopiquez, ruled that the alleged acts did not constitute a crime under the law.

“The CPP-NPA was not yet officially designated as a terrorist organization when the law RA 10168 was approved on June 18, 2012,” the judge said.

Inopiquez cited Section 15 of RA No. 10168 and Rules 15 (a) and (b) of its implementing rules and regulations which mandates the Department of Foreign Affairs and the Anti-Terrorism Council to publish the official list of designated persons and groups.

Under the law, designated persons or groups are those who are identified as terrorists, those who fund terrorists, or those identified as designated under the applicable United Nations Security Council Resolution or by another jurisdiction or supranational jurisdiction.

The court noted that it was only on December 5, 2017, that Proclamation No. 374 declared the CPP-NPA a terrorist organization and directed the Department of Foreign Affairs to publish the designation under RA No. 10168. On December 9, 2020, the Anti-Terrorism Council issued Resolution No. 12 (2020), designating the CPP-NPA as a terrorist organization.

Without the official publication of the designation, Inopiquez explained that the statutory requirement was not complied with at the time of the alleged crime, affecting the existence of the third element of the crime — that the recipient of funds reportedly used for terrorism were designated persons/entities.

“Absence of such statutory publication requirement pursuant to Section 15 of RA No. 10168 and its Implementing Rules and Regulations constitute a violation of the constitutional right to due process,” the court added.

News article not official publication

The prosecution had presented documents to argue that the CPP-NPA was already designated a terrorist organization as early as 2002. These include declarations from the United States, European Union, and New Zealand from 2002 to 2010.

The prosecution had also asserted the designation of the CPP-NPA as a terrorist organization was publicly reported in the Philippines through the publication of two articles in the Philippine Star in 2002.

The court threw out the argument, saying the Philippine Star article was not the kind of publication required under Section 15 of RA No. 10168.

“The Act and its implementing rules do not consider a reporter’s news piece about a foreign or supranational designation to be an official publication,” the judge said.

Inopiquez said the publication could not have met the statutory requirement as it was published before RA No. 10168 was approved in 2012.

“The law must first be approved and then follows the publication. The publication, a statutory requirement, must not precede the approval of the law,” he stressed.

Vindicated and unyielding

“The dismissal of the CERNET 27 case affirms a fundamental principle: serving poor and vulnerable communities is not terrorism. Development work, humanitarian assistance, and human rights advocacy must never be criminalized,” the NGO said in a statement on Monday evening, May 18.

For years, CERNET members reported facing intimidation, red-tagging, and other forms of harassment.

In 2021, Elena Tijamo, a member of the Central Visayas Farmers Development Center (FARDEC) – a member-organization of CERNET – was abducted from her home and whose remains were subsequently identified by her family members in a Manila hospital a year later.

In 2023, activists Dyan Gumanao, a former CERNET worker, and Armand Dayoha, a staff member at the Visayas Human Development Agency (VIHDA), were abducted at the Cebu pier and only released days later after allegedly being interrogated and coerced into admitting that they were communist rebels.

“Despite this victory, the threat to civic space remains. Even now, proposals such as the so-called ‘terror-grooming’ bill filed by fugitive Senator Ronald dela Rosa threaten to further expand the State’s power to target dissent, activism, and community organizing under the guise of counterterrorism,” CERNET said.

The NGO said it would pursue criminal, administrative, and civil actions against those who sought the “malicious and wrongful prosecution” of CERNET’s members.

“Those who orchestrated, enabled, and perpetuated these baseless accusations must be held accountable under the law,” said Oliver Gimenez, chairperson of the CERNET Board of Trustees.

The National Union of People’s Lawyers (NUPL), meanwhile, said the case showed the continuing weaponization of counterterrorism laws against humanitarian work and legitimate advocacy.

“These laws grant executive agencies sweeping powers with immediate and punitive consequences, often before any meaningful judicial scrutiny can take place,” read a NUPL statement on Tuesday, May 19.

The NUPL called on the justice department to dismiss or withdraw charges filed without sufficient legal basis or based on fabricated evidence. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Vantage Point] The balance-sheet war behind SOCOTECO II’s future
World.content:
This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article.

When operational control over a franchise area is transferred, reversing that decision is nearly impossible. That is why the analysis of the balance-sheet comparison between the Razon-linked IGNITE Power proposal and Meralco deserves a more in-depth investigation.

In our last Vantage Point newsletter, we asked whether the board of South Cotabato II Electric Cooperative, Inc. (SOCOTECO II) rushed too soon toward the Enrique Razon-Manny Pacquiao opportunity.

It would be interesting to know which bidder actually has the financial depth and operational capability to rehabilitate a regional electricity monopoly without inevitably passing the hidden risks back to consumers.

Electricity distribution is one of the most durable recurring-cash-flow businesses in the country, largely because customers can’t just leave the grid when they decide to pull the plug.

SOCOTECO II’s franchise area covers General Santos City, Sarangani province, and Tupi and Polomolok of South Cotabato.

When operational control over a franchise area is transferred, reversing that decision is nearly impossible. That is why the analysis of the balance-sheet comparison between the Razon-linked IGNITE Power proposal and the Manila Electric Company (Meralco) deserves a more in-depth investigation.

The IGNITE proposal was seen to provide an initial P4 billion, as well as P10 billion in investments over five years. On paper, those numbers are impressive. Infrastructure finance, however, is chock full of projects at launch that seemed plausible until refinancing pressure, challenges with execution, and debates over governance occurred years later.

In the reshuffling of utility companies, headline promises of investment are just the starting point. The real issue lies in determining who assumes the risk when projections don’t come to fruition.

Meralco’s size

Meralco is the country’s largest listed electricity distribution utility. Its bottom line reflects roughly P120.8 billion in revenues, P11.4 billion in core net income, and P19.6 billion in EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization). Its net debt-to-EBITDA ratio was approximately 1.7 times.

Those numbers are important because rebuilding infrastructure needs more than a one-time capital injection for utility rehabilitation. It needs the capacity to fund upgrades, absorb regulatory shocks, sustain collections, pay debt, and stabilize tariffs.

Meralco’s risks are visible. The company has substantial debt liabilities. But those risks are reflected in audited filings and public disclosures.

The harder question to answer is: What exactly are the comparable audited numbers behind the IGNITE proposal? Prime Infra boasts robust group-level financials, with roughly P55.9 billion in revenues and P37.6 billion in EBITDA for 2024. But that is at the Prime Infra group level, and not the balance sheet of IGNITE Power itself.

A group that has a wealthy parent doesn’t imply the bidding entity has the same balance-sheet capacity. Unless there are binding guarantees and enforceable funding obligations, the headline commitments remain projections rather than fully bankable obligations.

There is a significant difference between rehabilitating an existing utility and carving out its productive assets into a new operating entity while legacy obligations remain elsewhere. Rehabilitation means one structure preserves institutional continuity. Establishing a new entity potentially ring-fences future earnings while isolating older liabilities.

Critics describe the arrangement less as a partnership than as “a surrender of ownership.” The underlying concern is economic: Who ultimately controls the future cash flows generated by the franchise?

IGNITE massages public perception

The Razon-backed group seems to be deliberately shifting the balance-sheet size debate in its favor. Its subtext, however, is that utility rehabilitation is not simply a matter of identifying which bidder is bigger, richer, and more institutionally based.

IGNITE and SOCOTECO II officials have reiterated that the cooperative is not legally regarded as an “ailing” entity. The group’s defense hinges on the theory that member-consumer-owners actually — not just balance-sheet comparisons — should decide the fate of the cooperative at the end of the day through a referendum.

The challenge faced by SOCOTECO II, however, is not only whether the IGNITE proposal can work in theory. It’s whether the public has witnessed enough audited, entity-level financial transparency on which to base its decision to divest operational control of one of Mindanao’s most critical electricity franchises to have confidence.

In utility restructuring, confidence isn’t established through investment headlines, but through fact-checkable balance sheets, enforceable pledges of funding, and transparent governance structures.

IGNITE’s argument works politically more than financially.

In stressing that SOCOTECO II is legally not an “ailing cooperative” the Razon group paints its bid as less a corporate takeover and more a participatory partnership.

Its messaging is easier for people to buy, especially in Mindanao where fears that local control will be lost to big Manila-based conglomerates remain sensitive. IGNITE, in effect, is weaponizing this fear in its favor.

But from a forensic-finance perspective, this argument is incomplete. Democratic approval does not automatically answer broader questions of balance-sheet strength, operational control, future tariff pressures, governance rights, and long-term risk allocation.

Meralco’s advantage is bigger than size, but also transparency: its audited disclosures, operating history and regulatory track record are publicly available, while IGNITE’s submission is still dominated by commitments made and the general standing of the Razon group more than entity-level financial capacity.

I welcome your views on these and other issues where decisions made in power shape the country’s economic future. – Rappler.com

World.title: COA rules against insurance firms on P1.5-billion claim vs Pag-IBIG Fund

The dispute goes way back to 1985 when Pag-IBIG Fund entered into a combined fire insurance policy with a group of 43 insurance firms and terminated in 2013

MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Audit (COA) has ruled against a group of private insurance companies on a petition that the Home Development Mutual Fund (HDMF) or Pag-IBIG Fund should remit P1.503 billion in insurance premiums connected to a 1985 deal that ended in 2013.

In an en banc decision, the COA upheld the government corporation’s arguments that the insurance firms’ petition was defective.

“The petitioners failed to submit authenticated copies of the decisions, orders, arbitral award, and supporting documents. The veracity of the money claim is questionable and cannot be ascertained,” the COA said.

The dispute goes way back to 1985 when Pag-IBIG Fund entered into a Group Insurers Combined Fire Insurance Policy with the group of insurance firms or “insurance pool” which placed all properties mortgaged to Pag-IBIG under mandatory insurance coverage against fire and other risks.

In October 2013, then-Pag-IBIG chief executive officer Darlene Marie Beberabe (now the Solicitor General) notified the insurance firms that Pag-IBIG would terminate the fire insurance coverage once the contract ends on December 31, 2013.

The insurers opposed the move and sought arbitration.

In May 2016, an arbitration committee ruled, among others, that Pag-IBIG “validly exercised its right on behalf of its borrowers to no longer renew any existing individual one-year insurance policies under the 1985 Group Policy.”

It also held that Pag-IBIG Fund “validly exercised its right to no longer enroll new borrowers under the 1985 Group Policy.”

World.title: FACT CHECK: No paid protesters in May 13 rally vs VP Sara, Dela Rosa – ex-DOF official
World.content:
This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article.

Former finance undersecretary Cielo Magno says that while she attended the May 13 protest, she was not among the organizers of the event and there was no promise of a payout to those who attended the rally

Claim: Former finance undersecretary Cielo Magno and political vlogger Lovely Granada pocketed funds that were meant to be paid out to the minors who joined the May 13 rally against Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa and Vice President Sara Duterte.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A video bearing the claim was posted on Facebook on May 14 and has since garnered over 287,000 views, 16,600 reactions, 2,330 comments, and 4,800 shares.

In the video, a narrator claims several minors were recruited to join the protest with promises of being paid P1,000 each, but they ended up not being paid.

“So, saan napunta ‘yung pondo na naibigay sa inyo? … Pati maliit na halaga, binubulsa niyo. Kaya tuwang-tuwa kayo na nag-aaya sa mga rally kasi may funding tapos ibubulsa niyo lang. Bakit hindi niyo binigay, Cielo Magno, Lovely Granada? Kawawa naman ‘yung mga bata, nagrereklamo,” the narrator says.

(So, what happened to the funds given to you? It’s a small amount, but you still pocketed it. That’s why you were so happy inviting people to rallies, because there was funding, and then you just pocketed it. Why didn’t you give it, Cielo Magno, Lovely Granada? Poor kids, they are complaining.)

The video was uploaded by the Facebook page, “KUYA WARAY,” with a visible nickname, “Laurence llagas Luntaga.” It has over 110,000 followers and consistently posts pro-Duterte content.

The facts: Magno debunked the claim, saying that while she attended the May 13 protest, she was not among the organizers of the event and that no one was promised money to attend the rally.

“Lahat ng sumama sa rally natin last Wednesday ay organic. Makikita naman na ito ay mula sa iba’t ibang lehitimong organisasyon katulad ng Tindig Pilipinas, Sentro, Akbayan, Student Council Alliance of the Philippines at 1Sambayan. Marami rin kusang pumunta na hindi miyembro ng kahit anong organisasyon,” she told Rappler.

(Everyone who joined our rally last Wednesday was organic. It can be seen that they came from various legitimate organizations such as Tindig Pilipinas, Sentro, Akbayan, the Student Council Alliance of the Philippines, and 1Sambayan. Many also went voluntarily who are not members of any organization.)

She added that media coverage of the protest showed no minors participating in the rally.

“Ako ay hindi kasama sa mga organizers but pumunta dahil nakikiisa sa panawagan na litisin si Sara at hulihin si Bato. Kung susuriin ang mga video sa event mula sa iba’t ibang media outlet na nag-cover ng event, wala rin makikitang minor na nag-participate sa rally,” she added.

(I was not among the organizers, but I went because I support the call to prosecute Sara and arrest Bato. If you examine the videos of the event from various media outlets that covered the event, you will not see any minors who participated in the rally.)

May 13 protest: The false claim circulated after various progressive groups staged a protest outside the Senate compound on May 13 to call for Duterte’s conviction via an impeachment court and the arrest of Dela Rosa, who at the time was under the Senate’s protective custody after the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for the former police chief under the Duterte-era drug war. (READ: Bato dela Rosa’s escape: Timeline, analyses, opinions from experts).

As of Monday, May 18, the Senate has already convened as an impeachment court for Duterte’s trial, while Dela Rosa continues to evade arrest. – Reinnard Balonzo/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: FACT CHECK: Singer Lana del Rey not part of Duterte’s defense team
World.content:
This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article.

The American singer-songwriter is not a practicing lawyer and did not make any statement supporting the former president

Claim: Lawyer Lana Del Rey is working to secure former president Rodrigo Duterte’s “absolute freedom” as part of his defense team in the latter’s crimes against humanity case at the International Criminal Court (ICC).

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The quote card, posted on May 4, has already received 2,000 reactions, 179 comments, and 86 shares as of writing.



It shows a photo of singer-songwriter Del Rey wearing formal attire, beside Duterte’s portrait. The text on the image reads, “Atty. Lana Del Rey: ‘I will not rest. I will use every legal and political avenue available to secure his absolute freedom.’”

The post claims that the statement was made on April 28, citing MLGC News Online.



Additional text on the lower part of the graphic reads, “Let me be crystal clear: Rodrigo Duterte will not spend another day in confinement.”



“We are mobilizing resources across borders, from human rights advocates to national legal highest courts and beyond. We will not stop until he is exonerated and free. This is not just a defense; it’s a mission,” her team allegedly said.



The photo was posted in a Facebook group named “Sara Duterte Supporters” and prompted comments of gratitude from Duterte supporters.

The facts: The quote card is fake. The singer-songwriter is not a practicing lawyer, and she is not part of Duterte’s defense team. She did not make any statement supporting the former president, either.



A sparkle icon can also be seen at the bottom right corner of the graphic, indicating that it was generated using the artificial intelligence tool Google Gemini.



AI detection tool Sight Engine flagged the image as likely to be AI-generated. The image registered a score of 99.8% AI probability from Hive Moderation and a score of 97% AI probability from Undetectable AI.

Rappler has previously debunked similar false posts portraying personalities, even fictional characters, as Duterte supporters. These include posts featuring How to Get Away with Murder character Annalise Keating and Breaking Bad character Saul Goodman.

Vera Files has also fact-checked similar posts falsely claiming singer Sabrina Carpenter is part of Duterte’s defense team.



New lawyer: Duterte’s defense team was headed by British-Israeli lawyer Nicholas Kaufman, who represented the former president in his crimes against humanity case at the ICC. On May 8, Kaufman requested the ICC to remove him as Duterte’s lawyer, saying the former president expressed “his desire to hire replacement counsel.”

Duterte’s associate counsel, Dov Jacobs, also requested to leave the defense team, saying that Duterte’s reorganization is in preparation for the case’s trial phase.

On May 11, the ICC Trial Chamber III granted Kaufman’s request, while Jacobs’ request to withdraw was earlier approved on May 8.

International criminal and humanitarian law expert Peter Haynes is being eyed as Duterte’s new lawyer.

ICC case: On April 23, the ICC confirmed the charges against Duterte. This means that Duterte is going on trial, where prosecutors must prove that Duterte is guilty beyond reasonable doubt.

Duterte was arrested in March 2025 for charges of crimes against humanity due to his war on drugs campaign that killed over 30,000 individuals, according to rights groups.

A warrant of arrest for Senator Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa, who played a major role in the drug war as Duterte’s national police chief, has also been confirmed by the ICC.

Previous fact-checks: Rappler has previously fact-checked similar false claims about supposed statements of support for Duterte:

– Angelee Kaye Abelinde/Rappler.com

Angelee Kaye Abelinde is a student journalist based in Naga City, and an alumna of Rappler’s Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship 2024.

World.title: OpenAI defeats Elon Musk’s lawsuit, removes obstacle to IPO
World.content:
This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article.

TECH TYCOON. Tesla CEO Elon Musk boards Air Force One, as he travels with US President Donald Trump to New Jersey, at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, US, March 21, 2025.

Elon Musk says he will appeal, repeating his claim that OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and president Greg Brockman viewed OpenAI as a means to great wealth

CALIFORNIA, USA – A US jury on Monday, May 18, ruled against Elon Musk in his lawsuit against OpenAI, finding the artificial intelligence company not liable to the world’s richest person for allegedly straying from its original mission to benefit humanity.

In a unanimous verdict, the jury in Oakland, California, federal court said Musk brought his case too late. The jury deliberated less than two hours.

The three-week trial had widely been seen as a critical moment for the future of OpenAI and artificial intelligence generally, both in how it should be used and who should benefit from it.

The verdict simplifies the path for OpenAI to proceed with a possible initial public offering that could value the business at $1 trillion.

But OpenAI’s public face, chief executive Sam Altman, must also address challenges to his reputation from some personal testimony during the trial, including multiple witnesses describing him as a liar.

Musk said he will appeal, repeating his claim that Altman and OpenAI president Greg Brockman viewed OpenAI as a means to great wealth.

“Altman & Brockman did in fact enrich themselves by stealing a charity. The only question is WHEN they did it!” Musk posted on X. “Creating a precedent to loot charities is incredibly destructive to charitable giving in America.”

US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, who oversaw the trial, said in court after the verdict that Musk may face an uphill battle in an appeal, because whether the statute of limitations ran out before he sued was a factual issue.

“There’s a substantial amount of evidence to support the jury’s finding, which is why I was prepared to dismiss on the spot,” the judge said.

Musk invested early in OpenAI

In his lawsuit, Musk accused OpenAI, Altman and Brockman of manipulating him into giving $38 million, then going behind his back by attaching a for-profit business to its original nonprofit and accepting tens of billions of dollars from Microsoft MSFT.O and other investors.

Marc Toberoff, a lawyer for Musk, said the verdict could encourage other startups that begin as nonprofits but have greater ambitions to raise money, create for-profit entities to scale, and make their officers and directors rich.

“It’s a brand new formula for Silicon Valley,” he told reporters.

OpenAI was founded by Altman, Musk and several others in 2015. Musk left its board in 2018, and OpenAI set up a for-profit business the next year.

Musk has since founded his own artificial intelligence startup, xAI, which is now part of his SpaceX rocket and satellite company.

OpenAI countered that it was Musk who saw dollar signs, and waited too long to claim OpenAI breached its founding agreement to build safe artificial intelligence to benefit humanity.

Musk had a three-year statute of limitations to sue, and OpenAI’s lawyers said his August 2024 lawsuit came too late because he knew several years earlier about OpenAI’s growth plans.

Bill Savitt, a lawyer for OpenAI, told reporters after the verdict that Musk’s lawsuit was an “after-the-fact contrivance that bears no relationship to reality,” and a “hypocritical attempt to sabotage a competitor.”

Jurors, he said, “kicked it exactly where it belongs, which is to the side.”

Dan Ives, an analyst at Wedbush, said the verdict removed a significant overhang to a potential OpenAI IPO.

“This is a huge win for Altman and OpenAI despite the scrapes and bruises on Altman’s persona and leadership,” he said.

Monday’s verdict followed 11 days of testimony and arguments where Musk’s and Altman’s credibility came under repeated attack.

Microsoft had faced an aiding-and-abetting claim. A Microsoft executive testified that the company has spent more than $100 billion on its partnership with OpenAI.

“The facts and the timeline in this case have long been clear and we welcome the jury’s decision to dismiss these claims as untimely,” a Microsoft spokesperson said.

Candor, credibility at issue

People use AI for myriad purposes such as education, facial recognition, financial advice, journalism, legal research, medical diagnoses and harmful deepfakes.

Many people express distrust of the technology and worry it could displace people from their jobs.

Each side accused the other of being more interested in money than serving the public.

Musk said OpenAI failed to prioritize AI safety and wrongfully tried to enrich investors and insiders at the nonprofit’s expense. He also said Microsoft knew all along that OpenAI cared more about money than being altruistic.

Steven Molo, another Musk lawyer, reminded jurors in his closing argument that several witnesses questioned Altman’s candor or branded him a liar, and that Altman did not give an unqualified yes when asked during the trial if he was completely trustworthy.

“Sam Altman’s credibility is directly at issue,” Molo said. “If you don’t believe him, they cannot win.”

Sarah Eddy, another lawyer for the OpenAI defendants, accused Musk and his legal team in her closing argument of resorting to “sound bites and irrelevant false accusations.”

SpaceX is preparing an IPO that could exceed OpenAI’s in size. – Rappler.com

World.title: What do we know about the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus?
World.content:
This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article.

BUDDING. A digitally colorized scanning electron micrograph depiction shows numerous filamentous Ebola virus particles in green, budding from a chronically infected VERO E6 cell in orange at 25,000X magnification in this undated handout picture from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases.

Bundibugyo kills 30% to 40% of infected people, making it less lethal than the more common Zaire strain, which causes death in up to 90%, according to a 2024 global study

A rare strain of Ebola has prompted the World Health Organization to declare a public health emergency of international concern. Most cases have been reported in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with more than 100 suspected deaths and nearly 400 suspected infections as of Monday.

Here is what we know about the strain of Ebola virus known as Bundibugyo.

What is Bundibugyo Ebola?

The current Ebola outbreak, so far limited to the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda, is due to a rare strain of the virus known as Bundibugyo, named after Uganda’s Bundibugyo province where it was first identified during an outbreak in 2007-2008. A second Bundibugyo outbreak occurred in 2012 in the DRC.

Bundibugyo kills 30% to 40% of infected people, making it less lethal than the more common Zaire strain, which causes death in up to 90%, according to a global study published in 2024.

OUTBREAK. A man is carried from an ambulance as he arrives at Bunia General Referral Hospital following confirmation of an Ebola outbreak involving the Bundibugyo strain in Bunia, Ituri province, Democratic Republic of Congo, May 16, 2026. Reuters

Bundibugyo is one of the four species of the Ebolavirus genus that cause life-threatening illness in humans. All Ebola viruses are transmitted through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected animals or humans, or objects contaminated with such fluids.

Body fluid transmission is a particular risk for hospital workers. A US doctor working in the DRC has been infected in the current outbreak.

According to the World Health Organization, ebolaviruses initially cause flu-like symptoms including fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle pain, headache and sore throat that can start suddenly, followed by vomiting and diarrhea, and eventually internal and external bleeding and multi-organ failure.

Are there treatments for Bundibugyo?

There are no approved vaccines or drugs for Bundibugyo ebolavirus. Emergency use authorization would be necessary for deployment of any experimental treatments or existing therapies that have been effective against other strains.

Potential candidates that have helped to control Bundibugyo in trials in non-human primates include Merck’s Ervebo, Mapp Biopharmaceutical’s MBP 134, and Auro Vaccines’ VesiculoVax.

NanoViricides said its experimental antiviral drug NV-387, currently in clinical trials against mpox, could be effective against the Bundibugyo strain. It mimics immune cell surface proteins to which all ebolaviruses attach and could act as a decoy to “soak up” the virus and prevent it from attaching to healthy cells.

Earlier in the pipeline, an mRNA vaccine being developed in China has shown promise against Bundibugyo in mice but has not yet been tested in primates.

For now, response efforts will rely on public health measures such as rapid case detection, isolation, contact tracing, infection prevention and control, safe burials, and community engagement, said Dr. Daniela Manno of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine in a statement.

“These measures were critical in eventually controlling the 2014–2016 West Africa Ebola epidemic, the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded, and if implemented rapidly and effectively they can also help control this outbreak,” Manno said.

Is there a test for Bundibugyo?

Tests for Bundibugyo exist but are not widely used. Initial analysis of samples in the current outbreak using standard tests did not detect the infections.

“Because early tests looked for the wrong strain of Ebola, we got false negatives and lost weeks of response time,” Dr. Matthew Kavanagh, director of the Georgetown University Center for Global Health Policy & Politics in Washington, D.C., said in a statement.

“By the time the alarm was raised, the virus had already moved along major transport routes and crossed borders,” Kavanagh said.

What makes Bundibugyo different from other strains?

Differences in genetic makeup between Bundibugyo and other ebolaviruses impact its virulence, infectiousness, diagnosis, and the availability of medical treatments.

Compared to the Zaire strain, which quickly replicates to reach high levels in the patient’s body, Bundibugyo replicates more slowly.

Bundibugyo is also slower to invade, disable, and kill immune cells, eventually weakening the patient’s immune defenses.

The incubation periods for Bundibugyo virus and the Zaire virus are nearly identical, averaging 8 to 10 days but sometimes lasting up to three weeks.

A recent study of survivors of the 2007 Bundibugyo outbreak that found persistent symptoms and immune and metabolic alterations nevertheless concluded that overall Bundibugyo may have less severe long-term effects on the liver and kidneys than the Zaire strain. – Rappler.com

World.title: Court convicts KOJC member over Quiboloy arrest blockade
World.content:
Kingdom of Jesus Christ logo. — Photo from Philippine News Agency

*This story is being reposted to correct and rectify the improper use of the picture of pastor Apollo Quiboloy, and to clarify that he is not actually the person actually convicted in the case reported.

MANILA, Philippines — A Quezon City court has convicted a Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) member for violating the Public Assembly Act over a highway blockade staged during the 2024 police operations against televangelist Apollo Quiboloy.

The Metropolitan Trial Court Branch 39, Quezon City found Eduardo Corda guilty of violating Section 13(a) of Batas Pambansa Bilang 880, or the Public Assembly Act of 1985, in connection with protests conducted during the August 2024 standoff at the KOJC compound in Davao City.

Article continues after this 

In its ruling, shared by former Philippine National Police (PNP) chief and now Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) general manager Nicolas Torre III on his social media account on May 1, the court sentenced Corda to four months’ imprisonment.

Torre, in his caption, said, the decision is “not a celebration” nor “revenge,” but a reminder that “the law is the law.”

“Shouting cannot be used as a defense. Noise cannot be used as an exemption,” Torre wrote in Filipino.

He added that the ruling underscored accountability regardless of influence or status.

“If ordinary citizens are required to obey the law, those in power should do so even more,” he said.

Article continues after this 

Torre served as the Davao regional police chief during the 2024 standoff.

The case stemmed from protests and barricades mounted by KOJC supporters during attempts by authorities to serve arrest warrants against Quiboloy.

Article continues after this 

READ: Trafficking, abuse raps filed vs Quiboloy in Pasig, Davao

According to the decision, demonstrators occupied portions of the Philippine-Japan Friendship Highway using vehicles and other barricades, causing public obstruction during the police operations.

While the group had secured a permit for a “prayer rally and candle lighting” activity, the decision said it only covered an event strictly inside the “KOJC compound.”

“By barricading a national thoroughfare with heavy equipment, the participants exceeded the spatial authority granted. In this regard, a permit is not a license to occupy any public space at will; it is limited by the conditions and locations specified therein,” the court said.

Corda’s camp had argued during trial that he merely acted in a ministerial or peacekeeping role during the gathering and did not organize unlawful activities.

Defense witnesses also maintained that the protest was peaceful.

The decision, however, noted that authorities considered Corda among the leaders of the assembly, citing his use of a megaphone and crowd coordination during the standoff.

READ: 2,000 cops surround KJC complex, arrest warrant vs. Quiboloy served anew

The court emphasized that freedom of assembly is not absolute and may be regulated in the interest of public order.

“When the exercise of free expression transcends the bounds of its legal authorization and encroaches upon the fundamental right of the public to safe and unobstructed passage, the law provides for a necessary reckoning. This case stands as a testament to that delicate balance between individual liberty and collective security,” the ruling stated.

As of posting time, the defense’s team had yet to respond to Inquirer’s requests for comment.

The protests erupted during the high-profile police operations conducted in August 2024 to arrest Quiboloy.

Quiboloy was eventually taken into government custody in September 2024 after weeks of operations and negotiations. /das

World.title: NBI sends findings on Senate shooting to DOJ-Ombudsman probe team
World.content:
National Bureau of Investigation agents are seen in a video of the shooting in the Senate on Wednesday, May 13, 2026. (Screengrab from NBI-OTCD)

MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has submitted its findings on the shooting at the Senate last week to the panel investigating the incident.

“The Department of Justice and the Office of the Ombudsman already created a panel to investigate,” NBI director Melvin Matibag told reporters in Camp Crame on Tuesday.

“Today, we submitted a report, the findings of the NBI, but we reserve our right to submit additional findings,” he said.

Article continues after this 

The NBI chief declined to provide further details.

READ: Matibag: NBI driver may have gotten gunpowder in Senate premises

However, Matibag confirmed that the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG)– National Capital Region visited the NBI’s main office in Pasay City on Monday as part of the investigation.

As the session ended late Wednesday afternoon, dela Rosa had claimed that elements of the NBI and the CIDG were moving to arrest him.

Later that night, Senate security personnel supposedly spotted two individuals believed to be NBI agents who were carrying long firearms, according to an incident report sent by Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla to Senate President Alan Peter Cayetano.

Article continues after this 

When the purported NBI agents were asked to lower their guns but they defied the request, Senate Sergeant-at-Arms Mao Aplasca fired a “warning shot.” Several more gunshots were heard afterwards.

Senate security personnel had fired 27 shots, while the individuals believed to be NBI agents had fired five shots, according to Cayetano.

Article continues after this 

Matibag has since denied deploying agents to the Senate on Wednesday night, saying they were instead deployed to the Government Service Insurance System premises at the request of the latter for security measures. /apl

World.title: Over 1,100 PNP personnel penalized in internal cleansing drive
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — A total of 1,191 police officers have been penalized administratively from January 1 to May 6, 2026 as part of the national police force’s internal cleansing and disciplinary efforts, data from the Philippine National Police (PNP) showed.

The Directorate for Investigation and Detective Management (DIDM) said that among the penalties imposed were dismissal from service, suspension, demotion, forfeiture of salary, restriction, reprimand, and withholding of privileges.The sanctions were based on the gravity of the offenses and imposed in accordance with existing laws and regulations.

Among those penalized, 551 personnel were suspended, 353 were dismissed from service, 176 faced salary forfeiture, 63 were demoted, 23 received reprimands, 20 had privileges withheld, and five were placed under restriction.In a statement on Tuesday, PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. emphasized that disciplinary actions are enforced regardless of rank or position as part of the organization’s efforts to preserve accountability and institutional integrity.

Article continues after this 

“It is important that we maintain public trust through a disciplined and professional police force,” Nartatez said in Filipino.

Separate records from the DIDM showed that from August 26, 2025 to May 6, 2026, a total of 1,108 personnel were dismissed from service under the PNP’s intensified disciplinary drive.

The figure included 1,020 Police Non-Commissioned Officers, 52 Police Commissioned Officers, and 36 Non-Uniformed Personnel, reflecting the PNP’s policy of accountability across all ranks.

READ: PNP touts internal cleansing, recruitment reforms vs ‘ninja cops

Earlier, the PNP strengthened its internal cleansing and recruitment reforms targeting “ninja cops” involved in the resale of seized illegal drugs. /gsg

World.title: 7 Pangasinan barangays get tractors under tobacco excise tax fund
World.content:
The Villasis municipal government in Pangasinan turns over tractors to selected barangays under its tobacco excise tax-funded agricultural support program, aimed at boosting farm productivity and improving farmers’ livelihoods. (Photo courtesy of Villasis LGU)

VILLASIS, Pangasinan — The local government unit (LGU) here has turned over seven tractors worth about P1.356 million each to seven barangays in this agricultural town, funded through tobacco excise tax revenues.

The beneficiary barangays are Lipay, San Blas, Unzad, Labit, Bacag, Tombod, and Amamperez.

This marks the third consecutive year that the municipal government has distributed tractors to villages. In 2025, the LGU also turned over six tractors to six barangays, while two units were earlier awarded to farmers’ associations a year before.

Article continues after this 

READ: Rice farmers get P400M worth of agri machinery

Some barangays opted to receive alternative support such as solar power generators, other farm equipment, and farm-to-market road projects, also funded by the tobacco excise tax.

Mayor Dita Abrenica said the turnover on May 14 is part of the town’s continuing program to support local farmers and strengthen agricultural productivity.

She added that investments in farm machinery and agricultural programs aim to improve farm output and enhance livelihood opportunities for farmers.

Abrenica said Villasis received a total of P46 million from tobacco excise tax allocations.

Article continues after this 

READ: PH loses P25B annually on illicit tobacco trade

Municipal Agriculture Officer Dionisio Cariño said barangay officials will be responsible for the maintenance and management of the tractors.

Article continues after this 

He added that the barangays will oversee the lending system for farmers, with rental fees set lower than prevailing market rates.

Known as the vegetable bowl of Pangasinan, Villasis also produces native tobacco locally known as “batek” and burley tobacco after the rice harvest season./coa

World.title: Prosecutors raring to present evidence in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
World.content:
Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro and other lawmakers huddle after a short break before voting on the opening of the box containing income tax records of Vice President Sara Duterte provided by the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) to the House Justice Committee during impeachment hearing at the House of Representatives in Quezon City on Wednesday, April 29, 2026. INQUIRER PHOTO / GRIG C. MONTEGRANDE

MANILA, Philippines — Members of the House of Representatives’ prosecution team are raring to present evidence in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, saying they will carry out their mandate seriously and with “respect for the process.”

In a statement on Tuesday, Manila Rep. Joel Chua said that the prosecution team acknowledges the Senate’s move on Monday to convene itself as an impeachment court for Duterte’s trial.

“We acknowledge the convening of the Senate impeachment court for the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte,” Chua, a member of the 11-person prosecution team, said. “We are prepared to present the evidence before the impeachment court and to comply with its lawful orders, directives and procedures.”

Article continues after this 

“As members of the House prosecution panel, we look forward to performing our mandate under the Constitution with seriousness, discipline and respect for the process,” he added. “This is a constitutional duty entrusted to the House of Representatives, especially in matters involving accountability of impeachable public officers.”

Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon in a separate interview on Monday night said that they will comply with the orders that will be issued by the Senate Impeachment Court, and reply immediately once Duterte answers the articles of impeachment.

The Senate impeachment court gave Duterte 10 calendar days to answer the articles against her. The prosecution team, on the other hand, will be given five calendar days to counter this answer from Duterte.

“We saw that they formally convened the Senate Impeachment Court, we thank the Senate for convening the Senate Impeachment Court and the prosecution panel of the House is preparing for any other orders that may be issued,” Ridon said in Filipino.

“So as soon as the Vice President submits her answer, the House panel will provide a reply to her answer. I think this is the final opportunity of the Vice President to provide a most-complete defense. So our expectation would be that they will raise the previous jurisdictional questions or constitutional questions in their answer, but also provide a more substantial reply,” he added.

Article continues after this 

Currently, Chua said that the prosecution’s immediate task is to ensure that the evidence is properly heard and tested.

“At this stage, our duty is clear: to help ensure that the facts are heard, the evidence is tested and the process is carried out in a manner worthy of the trust of the Filipino people,” he noted.

Article continues after this 

Despite the recent turmoil within the Senate, the chamber convened itself as an impeachment court, with Senate President Alan Peter Cayetano taking an oath as the presiding judge, and the remaining 22 senators present being sworn as senator-judges.

The convening of the impeachment court came a week after the House impeached Duterte, with 257 House lawmakers voting in favor of adopting House Resolution (HR) No. 989 which contains Committee Report No. 261 and the articles of impeachment.

After the Senate convened itself, the prosecution team formally made its entry of appearance, assigning House committee on justice chairperson and Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro as the lead public prosecutor.

READ: Senate convenes as impeachment court

Prior to Duterte’s impeachment, three clarificatory hearings were held to discuss the grounds stated in the two remaining impeachment complaints. Last April 14, the panel discussed allegations of confidential fund (CF) misuse within the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd), which she used to head before.

Some of the revelations made during the April 14 hearing were contained in the supplemental affidavit of Ramil Madriaga, Duterte’s former aide.

According to Madriaga, Duterte supposedly ordered her in December 2022 to deliver cash to allies as a way of “giving back.” Madriaga said four large duffle bags were unloaded from the vehicles, three of them were dark and one was light-colored — containing around P30 million to P35 million each.

This is believed to be the P125 million confidential fund in 2022, which Madriaga said he liquidated in one day and not the reported 11 days.

READ: Madriaga: OVP’s 2022 secret funds spent in 1 day, not 11 days

On April 22, the panel tackled accusations that Duterte has unexplained wealth, and that she failed to disclose all her assets in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth.

At one point during the hearing, Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Buenaventura confirmed that they saw covered and suspicious transactions made by Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio.

Later on, Mamamayang Liberal party-list Rep. Leila de Lima randomly picked 19 transactions posted in Senator Antonio Trillanes IV’s affidavit against Duterte, asking if this would match the records at AMLC’s hand.

Buenaventura said that 19 out of the 19 transactions identified by de Lima were confirmed to be part of AMLC’s records.

READ: Trillanes vindicated: AMLC confirms Sara Duterte’s 18 transactions

On April 29, the committee tackled Duterte’s threats against ranking officials, with the National Bureau of Investigation authenticating video clips containing the Vice President’s rants against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former House Speaker Ferdinand Martin Romualdez.

After some discussions on Monday, the Senate convened the impeachment court, issuing summons to Duterte asking for her response to the articles of impeachment.

World.title: NBI has many leads on dela Rosa’s whereabouts, says Matibag
World.content:
National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag (Photo from NIÑO JESUS ORBETA / Inquirer)

MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has several information on the whereabouts of Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa following his exit from the Senate building, NBI Director Melvin Matibag revealed on Tuesday.

But Matibag refused to provide details on dela Rosa’s location, citing the bureau’s investigation process.

“There have been so many leads given. We have a lead on where he is. But in the meantime, we have to suspend the announcement on where he is,” the NBI chief said during the Machra’s Balitaan on Tuesday.

Article continues after this

He earlier said that Padilla is considered a “person of interest” who can shed light on dela Rosa’s whereabouts.

READ: Padilla is a ‘person of interest’ in dela Rosa’s escape from Senate – NBI

The senator’s departure took place hours after the shooting between the Senate Office of the Sergeant-at-Arms and NBI agents on Wednesday evening.

Dela Rosa is among the personalities tagged as co-perpetrators in the crimes against humanity case filed against former President Rodrigo Duterte before the ICC, as he served as the Philippine National Police chief from 2016 to 2018.

World.title: Cebu court dismisses terrorism financing case vs NGO officials
World.content:
A Cebu City court has dismissed the terrorism financing case filed against officials and members of the Community Empowerment Resource Network, Inc. (CERNET), ruling that the alleged acts were not punishable under the law at the time they were supposedly committed. INQUIRER FILE PHOTO

TACLOBAN CITY — A Cebu City court has dismissed the terrorism financing case filed against officials and members of the Community Empowerment Resource Network, Inc. (CERNET), ruling that the alleged acts were not punishable under the law at the time they were supposedly committed.

In a 13-page decision promulgated on May 15, Judge Van Russel Inopiquez of the Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 74 in Cebu City dismissed the charges against all accused, involving 27 individuals, for “lack of statutory publication requirement.”

The accused were charged under Section 8(ii), in relation to Section 9, of Republic Act No. 10168, or the Terrorism Financing Prevention and Suppression Act, filed on May,2023 by the military belonging to the 302nd Infantry Brigade based in Tanjay City, Negros Oriental.

Article continues after this 

READ: Cebu’s Red-tagged NGO asks gov’t to stop harassment as trial looms

The military alleged that CERNET was involved in a fund generation scheme to the NPA involving P135,000 in Dumaguete City in September 2012, just months after the law took effect on June 18 of the same year.

CERNET is a registered non-stock, non-profit development organization based in Cebu that works with people’s organizations composed of farmers, fisherfolk, and urban poor communities in Cebu, Negros Oriental, Bohol, and Siquijor, and some parts of the Visayas.

In dismissing the case, the court noted that Section 15 of RA 10168 requires the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) to publish a list of designated persons or organizations before such designation can take legal effect in the Philippines.

The court noted that no such publication existed in September 2012, when the alleged transaction took place. It added that the first official domestic designation of the NPA as a terrorist organization under Proclamation No. 374 was issued only on December 5, 2017.

Article continues after this 

“RA 10168 was just passed in 2012. The purported 2002 publication could not have met the statutory requirement as provided in Section 15 of RA 10168. The law must first be approved and then followed by the publication,” the court said in its ruling.

It further stated that “the acts charged do not constitute an offense under the law in force at the time of their commission.”

Article continues after this 

READ: Cebu court sets trial for 24 red-tagged NGO workers

The prosecutor had claimed that as early as 2002, the NPA, the armed group of the Communist Party of the Philippines, had been designated as a terrorist group by the United States and European Union, using newspaper articles as support.

The ruling was welcomed by the National Union of People’s Lawyers (NUPL), which said the case reflected the alleged misuse of counterterrorism laws against humanitarian and development organizations.

“The case highlights the continuing weaponization of counterterrorism laws against humanitarian work and legitimate advocacy,” NUPL said in a statement.

“These laws grant executive agencies sweeping powers with immediate and punitive consequences, often before any meaningful judicial scrutiny can take place,” it added.

World.title: Senate shooting suspect says he never held gun, cites video footage
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) volunteer driver tagged in last week’s Senate shooting on Tuesday denied firing or even holding a gun on the day of the incident as captured in a video footage and wonders why he tested positive for gunpowder residue after a paraffin test.

He said he never handled a gun since arriving at the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) complex on the day of the shooting incident.

“‘Yun na nga po, maam. Nagtaka po ako kasi never po akong humawak ng baril noong araw na yun hanggang makarating kami dun, makabalik ako.”

Article continues after this 

(That’s exactly why I was puzzled, ma’am, because I never handled a gun that day from the time we arrived there until I returned.)

“May video po na magpapatunay na wala po akong dalang baril,” Oragon added.

(There is a video clip that can prove I was not carrying a gun.)

The Southern Police District (SPD) earlier identified “Oragon” as the lone suspect in the May 13 gunfire incident involving personnel from the Senate’s Office of the Sergeant-at-Arms (OSAA) and the NBI stationed at the GSIS building.

The Senate and the GSIS buildings sit adjacent to each other, both being within the GSIS complex.

Article continues after this 

Days after his arrest, Oragon tested positive for gunpowder residue in a paraffin test, although the SPD said the result was not conclusive proof that he had fired a gun and that the investigation remains ongoing.

NBI Director Melvin Matibag previously clarified that Oragon was not an official employee of the bureau but merely served as a volunteer driver during the operation at the GSIS complex.

Article continues after this 

Told to retrieve bag, arrested

“Oragon” reiterated that their team had only been instructed to “stand by,” monitor the situation, and “walang ibang gagawin” (not do anything else), while stationed in a vehicle.

They later heard successive gunshots from the area and were told to remain on standby for around 30 minutes before being ordered to proceed to the ground floor.

He said the later returned to the NBI office for a briefing following the shooting incident when he was informed that a bag had accidentally been left behind.

“Biglang tinawag at sinabihan ako na may naiwang bag, isa sa kasamahan natin na kailangan makuha dahil may mga gamot na laman. Kailangan ng may-ari. So wala akong agam agam na sinunod yung utos. At bumalik ako mag-isa. Dala yung aking personal na motorsiklo doon sa GSIS building,” he said.

(I was suddenly called and told that a bag had been left behind by one of our companions and needed to be retrieved because it contained medicines needed by its owner. So without hesitation, I followed the instruction and returned alone, using my personal motorcycle to go back to the GSIS building,)

Upon his return, Oragon recounted that guards at the GSIS premises allowed him entry after he identified himself as “Oragon from NBI,” a name “na nakatimbre na” (that had already been endorsed) at the gate.

He said it was around between 9:00 and 10:00 when he returned and a security guard escorted him to the second floor.

“Biglang may sumalubong sa akin na pulis at tinanong kung sino ako… tinanong niya ako, anong ginagawa ko doon. Sabi ko, ‘Sir, may hinahanap lang po akong bag na naiwan,’” he said.

(Suddenly, a police officer approached me and asked who I was… he asked me what I was doing there. I told him, ‘Sir, I’m just looking for a bag that was left behind,’)

Authorities later arrested him.

Asked about the ammunition and bags allegedly recovered from him during his arrest, Oragon said, “Nagulat nga po ako na inuugnay sa akin dahil never ko pong nahawakan o nalapitan yung bag.”

(I was surprised that I was being linked to it because I never touched or even got close to the bag)

Oregon said he has served as an NBI volunteer since 2016 and is also a reservist of the Philippine Army.

He added that he receives no regular salary for his volunteer work and usually survives through occasional allowances and his wife’s income.

Aftermath of arrest

He admitted that the incident has taken a heavy emotional toll on his family.

Oragon was later released after posting P116,000 bail – P80,000 for alleged violation of Republic Act No. 10591, or the Comprehensive Firearms and Ammunition Regulation Act, and P36,000 for direct assault.
